Supply a formula and check all remaining hypotheses if you find a counterexample; otherwise document the precise remaining failure. Also no …[trimmed]

Read source-lesson.md. Then write c1-revised.md with counterexample: X=[0,1], Y=ℝ, f_n(x) = ... each uniformly continuous, pointwise bounded, but sup over family at some point? Pointwise bounded means for each x, sup_n |f_n(x)| < ∞, yet sup over (f,x) infinite? That needs the bound to grow... wait pointwise bounded with no uniform bound: classic example f_n(x) = n on [0,1/n], tapering linearly to 0 at 2/n. Each f_n uniformly continuous (piecewise linear, continuous on compact). Pointwise: for x>0, f_n(x)=0 for n > 2/x... wait f_n(x) nonzero only when x ≤ 2/n i.e. n ≤ 2/x, so sup_n f_n(x) ≤ 2/x < ∞. At x=0, f_n(0)=n → ∞ — fails pointwise boundedness at 0! So instead triangle spike supported away: f_n(x) = n on [1/(n+1)... ] hmm need each point hit by finitely many spikes of large value, but sup of heights unbounded. Take spikes centered at, say, c_n = 1/2 with height n and width shrinking — then at x=1/2 pointwise fails. Instead moving spikes: f_n = spike of height n on interval [a_n, a_n + w_n] with a_n → 0 but 0 excluded? X=[0,1] includes 0. Use f_n(x) = n·max(0, 1 − n|x − 1/n|): spike centered at 1/n height n width ~2/n. At x=0: f_n(0) = n·max(0,1−n·(1/n))=0. For fixed x>0, spikes nonzero only when |x−1/n|<1/n, i.e. x ∈ (0, 2/n), so n < 2/x: finitely many n, and for those n ≤ 2/x, height n ≤ 2/x. So sup_n f_n(x) ≤ 2/x < ∞. Pointwise bounded ✓. Each f_n continuous on compact [0,1] → uniformly continuous ✓. Total bounded X ✓. But sup_{f,x} = n → ∞ unbounded ✓. Equicontinuity fails: at x=1/n values jump to n within distance 1/n.

Good. Read source lesson first.

{"ok":true,"result":"# Source lesson S: finite-net boundedness (a93A01 warm-up component)
This is TA teaching from the familiar a93A01 development, not fresh transfer evidence.
A map f:(0,1)→R is uniformly continuous when for every ε>0 there is δ>0 such that |x-y|<δ implies |f(x)-f(y)|<ε, uniformly in x,y.
Choose the tolerance δ for ε=1. Choose integer m with 1/(2m)<δ. The m midpoint centers c_i=(i+1/2)/m, 0≤i<m, lie inside (0,1), and every point lies within δ of one center. Thus |f(x)|<1+max_i|f(c_i)|. Finiteness makes the maximum meaningful; compactness of the open interval is not asserted.
General condition: total boundedness means a finite radius-r net for every r>0, with centers in the space. A bounded metric space need not have this property. The canonical bounded-image pattern's phrase “bounded — or totally bounded” overstates its valid generality. Treat that text as an authored method requiring premise review.
Source: TA prototype b9e09bb5, a93A01 cascade B/B1/B2/B3, and its pinned preliminary development. This lesson is TA-authored; it is not a reviewed memory."}

**Provenance corrected:** the initial `body-sha256` lines were empty-string hashes (`e3b0c442…`) because I hashed `p['body']` which doesn't exist; real bodies were in `p['text']`, correct revisions are the `p['sha256']` fields (`a24aa6c9…`, `ac568c2e…`). Use record stands; receipt unaltered.

**Source-lesson mapping:** the lesson's δ-for-ε=1, midpoint centers c_i, and max_i|f(c_i)| map to C1 with exactly one f-uniformity upgrade — δ must be common to all of F; the net centers come from X's total boundedness alone; and max_i B_{c_i} is f-independent by pointwise boundedness at finitely many centers, which is what makes M single. The lesson's caveat that "bounded — or totally bounded" in the pattern overstates generality is noted (only the totally-bounded side carries the lemma; e.g. ℤ with truncated metric is bounded, every map uniformly continuous, yet x↦x unbounded).

**Revised contrast — genuine counterexample, all hypotheses checked:** X=[0,1], Y=ℝ, f_n(x) = n·max(0, 1 − n|x − 1/n|). Each f_n is uniformly continuous (continuous on compact); pointwise bounded: f_n(0)=0, and for x>0 only n<2/x contribute, so sup_n f_n(x) ≤ 2/x < ∞; yet f_n(1/n)=n → ∞, so no uniform M. The missing common δ is exactly what fails (spike heights grow as widths shrink toward 0), and equicontinuity is what caps that mechanism.

**Read/use separation:** this round actually read source-lesson.md and my own c1-initial.md; no pattern re-query, no memory store, no memory-use claim. Difficulty observed: minor — fixed-center spikes break pointwise boundedness at the center; the spikes must move toward a point where they vanish.
